stories.headline: Eight Antifa Members Sentenced to Collective 450 Years for Anti-ICE Riot in Which Officer Was Shot
stories.summary:
A federal judge sentenced eight people with alleged ties to Antifa to a combined 450 years in prison Tuesday for their roles in a July 4, 2025, riot outside an immigration detention center in Prairieland, Texas. Benjamin Hanil Song, described by prosecutors as the group's leader and convicted of attempted murder of a law enforcement officer, received 100 years; sentences for the remaining seven ranged from 30 to 70 years. The defendants were convicted on charges including rioting, use of weapons and explosives, providing material support to terrorists, and obstruction.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that the sentences demonstrated violent attackers of law enforcement and federal facilities would face "swift and uncompromising justice." The presiding judge called the July 4 assault "an assault on democracy." A ninth defendant is scheduled for sentencing on July 1, along with seven others who pleaded guilty before trial.

Defendants' families and supporters condemned the sentences as disproportionate. Song wrote in a statement that he fired his weapon because he believed an officer was about to shoot a protester; his mother disputed that he shot anyone and said he did not intend to harm anyone, according to the Associated Press. Advocacy groups for the defendants characterized the punishments as unduly harsh.

The case carries broad political significance. President Trump designated Antifa a domestic terrorist organization in 2025, and the Justice Department framed the convictions as part of a broader effort against what it described as a network seeking to overthrow the government and law enforcement. Critics on the left argued the sentences reflect an aggressive use of terrorism statutes against political protesters.

stories.headline: New Fed Chair Warsh Retreats From Decades of Transparency, Risking Higher Rates and Market Volatility
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over the central bank earlier this year, is sharply curtailing the Fed's communications with financial markets, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater transparency. At his first press conference last week, Warsh stripped the central bank's post-meeting statement of forward guidance — signals about future interest-rate moves — that markets had relied upon to anticipate Fed policy. His approach echoes that of former Chair Alan Greenspan, who died Monday at 100 and was the only predecessor Warsh praised at his swearing-in.

Analysts warn the shift carries tangible economic risks. Without clear Fed signals, bond and stock markets may swing more sharply, and borrowing costs for consumers and businesses could rise modestly — perhaps a quarter-point on mortgage rates, according to George Pearkes, global macro strategist at Bespoke Investment Group. Pearkes said forward guidance has historically "suppressed volatility and anchored market expectations," leading to lower borrowing costs.

Warsh has argued that markets have become too dependent on Fed direction and that such guidance is better reserved for financial crises or severe downturns. His philosophy represents a philosophical break from the approach of recent chairs, who moved toward greater openness in part at Congress's urging. The practical test will come at future Fed meetings as investors are left to interpret rate decisions without the roadmaps they have grown accustomed to.

The transition comes at a consequential moment, with inflation and the tariff-driven economic outlook already creating uncertainty. The Fed's independence has also been a source of tension with the Trump administration. How markets absorb Warsh's more opaque style in the coming months will be closely watched as a signal for whether reduced transparency measurably raises the cost of credit for households and businesses.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Claims Vandalism at Reflecting Pool, Says 13 Arrested or Cited — AP Finds Evidence Contradicts Account
stories.summary:
President Trump escalated his claims Tuesday that vandals deliberately damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, asserting on social media that six people had been arrested and seven cited for causing a "350-foot gash" in the freshly painted liner — though he provided no supporting evidence and said images would be released to prove his account. The $14-million rehabilitation project drained the century-old pool, painted its bottom a color Trump called "American flag blue," and became a focal point of preparations for the nation's 250th anniversary celebration next week.

The Associated Press, which verified events at the site, found that one man was arrested after briefly touching paint that was already peeling — he said he wanted to examine the new coating and released a still-attached chunk shortly after a park worker told him to stop. The U.S. Park Police and Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment on Trump's specific arrest claims. National Guard members and Park Police have been deployed around the pool's deck after Trump began blaming vandals over the weekend.

The pool has been beset by problems since its restoration, including persistent algae blooms and visible peeling of the new liner coating. Scientists and critics have pointed to the paint formula and application as contributing factors. Trump has consistently attributed the deterioration to deliberate sabotage, saying "somebody had to work very hard, probably in the dark of night, to create such a condition."

The episode has become politically charged ahead of July 4 celebrations. Supporters of the renovation defend it as a patriotic upgrade to a national landmark, while critics argue the project was rushed, poorly executed, and that unsubstantiated vandalism claims are being used to deflect accountability for a flawed renovation funded by taxpayers.

stories.headline: Update: France Confirms First Ebola Case in Europe as Congo Outbreak Surpasses 1,000 Infections
stories.summary:
France has confirmed its first case of Ebola, involving a doctor who returned from a humanitarian mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The physician was immediately admitted to a specialized medical facility and is reported to be in stable condition, according to the French health ministry. Authorities stressed the risk to the general public remains "very low" and are working to trace any contacts the doctor may have had.

The case marks the first confirmed Ebola infection on European soil, though an American doctor who tested positive in DRC was treated at a German hospital last month. The ongoing outbreak in DRC has now surpassed 1,000 infections and claimed more than 260 lives, with cases concentrated in the eastern provinces of Ituri, South Kivu, and North Kivu. Neighboring Uganda has also recorded 20 infections and two deaths.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, for which no approved vaccine currently exists, complicating containment efforts. The World Health Organization has warned that active conflict in eastern DRC, where the M23 rebel group controls large areas, is significantly hampering the public health response. Africa CDC and U.S. public health authorities have described the outbreak as having the potential to become one of the largest ever recorded.

France has established a dedicated monitoring system for aid workers returning from DRC and confirmed it is conducting contact tracing. The confirmation of a European case is likely to intensify pressure on international health bodies to accelerate response funding and logistics, particularly as previous U.S. foreign aid cuts — including USAID reductions — have been cited as hampering on-the-ground containment work in DRC.

stories.headline: Update: European Heatwave Intensifies as France Records Hottest June Day Ever, 40 Dead
stories.summary:
France recorded its hottest average June day since records began on Tuesday, with a mean temperature of 29.8°C and peaks of 44.3°C in the Landes region. Red heat alerts have been extended to 58 of France's regions, with 31 additional regions under orange alert. The extreme heat has caused the country's first major heat-related power outage, leaving around 68,000 homes in Brittany without electricity, with full restoration not expected until end of day Wednesday.

At least 40 people have drowned in heatwave-related incidents in France since last Thursday, according to the French prime minister. Temperatures of 39–43°C are forecast across much of western France, from Paris to Brittany, through the weekend. The Louvre museum in Paris announced it would close two hours early each day through Saturday due to the heat in its historic building.

The heatwave is spreading across western Europe, with orange danger alerts issued for the Netherlands, while Germany is forecast to see temperatures reach 40°C over the weekend. Severe heat warnings have been extended to Poland, Croatia, and Hungary for later in the week. A major wildfire in the Maine-et-Loire region required more than 150 firefighters before being brought under control overnight.

The new material developments — France's record temperatures, the 40 drowning deaths, the mass power outage, and the heatwave's spread into northern and eastern Europe — represent a significant escalation from prior coverage. French labor minister Jean-Pierre Farandou said the country is "in the process of finding out we've become a hot country." Some relief is forecast from Friday, accompanied by risks of flash flooding and large hail from thunderstorms.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Drone Strike Blacks Out Sevastopol as Crimea Faces Fuel Shortages
stories.summary:
Ukrainian drones struck the main power substation of Sevastopol overnight, knocking out electricity across Russia's largest occupied city in Crimea. Moscow-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhayev warned some areas would remain without power until Wednesday evening and placed all emergency services on full alert. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces commander confirmed the attack was part of a broader overnight operation targeting 48 military sites.

The attack comes as Crimea is already under severe strain from a Ukrainian campaign to isolate the peninsula. All petrol sales have been suspended by Russian-installed authorities and reserved largely for government services, while panic-buying of basic goods has been reported in local shops. Kyiv has also targeted key bridges and road links connecting Crimea to mainland Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's defense ministry said it destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine's air force reported intercepting 95 of 101 Russian drones launched against Ukrainian territory. The intensified Ukrainian campaign against Crimean infrastructure is part of Kyiv's broader strategy of damaging Russian energy revenues and compelling Moscow to engage in negotiations. Sevastopol is a strategically vital port city and serves as a key logistical hub for Russian forces in the region.

Explosions were also reported in Bakhchisarai, Kerch, and near Mount Ai-Petri, where a Russian Aerospace Forces communications battalion is based. The strikes mark an escalation in Ukraine's pressure on occupied Crimea and come as fighting continues on multiple fronts in eastern Ukraine, where Russian troops have infiltrated the strategic city of Kostyantynivka.

stories.headline: Alibaba Sues Pentagon to Fight Military Blacklist That Would Sever U.S. Legal and Business Ties
stories.summary:
Chinese tech and e-commerce giant Alibaba has filed a lawsuit in a California federal court challenging its placement on the Pentagon's "1260H" blacklist, which designates companies deemed to be linked to China's military. The U.S. Department of Defense placed Alibaba on the list on the grounds that its compliance with Chinese technology regulators makes it effectively an arm of the Chinese military-civil fusion apparatus. Alibaba called the designation "arbitrary and capricious" and said it has "no basis in fact or law."

The practical stakes are acute: starting June 30, the Pentagon is legally barred from doing business with blacklisted firms, and — critically — the restriction extends to any U.S. contractor that shares a lobbyist or law firm with a blacklisted entity. Alibaba argues this effectively forces its American legal and political advisers to sever ties in order to protect their own defense contracts, stripping the company of representation in Washington at the precise moment it needs to fight back. The company says it previously sought a meeting with the DoD to present evidence of its U.S. economic contributions but received no response and no hearing before being designated.

Alibaba pushed back on the military affiliation claim, noting that all multinationals operating in China — including American companies — must comply with local regulations, and that none of its independent board members has any military ties. The company's platforms, it said, are built for retail and cloud computing, not defense or intelligence purposes. The DoD declined to comment on the litigation.

The case is part of a broader U.S. government effort to restrict Chinese technology firms: Baidu, BYD, and Nio are among other major companies recently added to the expanded blacklist. The outcome could set an important legal precedent for how U.S. regulators may designate foreign companies under national security statutes and how those companies may challenge such designations in court.
